read.sections.0.heading.source: A thing can connect several places
read.sections.0.heading.back: One object can link many places

read.sections.0.text.source:
Objects can connect distant societies through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, or objects made of fired clay, are useful evidence. Fired clay survives well, and vessels were made in large numbers. Their histories connect artistic decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Southeast Asian makers took an active part in these networks.

A Vietnamese dish in The Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. It is dated to the early sixteenth century. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong Province. This is an attribution, a reasoned identification of where it was made. The bird is painted in cobalt blue under a transparent glaze, a glass-like coating. The free brushwork shows a practised skill in decorating many vessels.

The dish was recovered from the cargo of the Hoi An shipwreck, near central Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s. It showed how large Vietnamese production of glazed ceramics had been.
read.sections.0.text.note: attribution uses the KEY_TERMS word การระบุผู้สร้าง, but here it is about WHERE the dish was made, so I wrote การระบุผู้สร้างหรือที่มาของงาน. A reviewer may prefer การระบุที่มา for this course. cargo chosen as สินค้าบรรทุก (not in KEY_TERMS). Stoneware as เครื่องหิน. Place names: ไหเซือง (Hải Dương), ฮอยอัน (Hội An).
read.sections.0.text.back:
Objects can connect distant societies through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, or things made of fired clay, are useful evidence: fired clay lasts a long time, and vessels were produced in large numbers. Their histories connect artistic decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Makers in Southeast Asia played an active role in these networks.

A Vietnamese dish in the Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. It dates to the early 16th century. The museum says it was probably made in Hai Duong province. This is an attribution, or statement of origin, a reasoned statement of where the work was made. The bird is painted in cobalt blue under a clear glaze, a glass-like coating. The freely drawn brushstrokes show skill practised by decorating many vessels.

This dish was found in the cargo of a shipwreck at Hoi An, near central Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s and shows how much glazed pottery Vietnam produced.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Objects can link places that are far apart. People make them, carry them, trade them and use them. Ceramics are things made of baked clay. They are good evidence. Baked clay lasts a long time. And people made very many of them. Makers in Southeast Asia played a big part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York shows a bird in clouds. It is from the early 1500s. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong, in Vietnam. This is an attribution. It is a careful, reasoned idea of where it was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny coat, like glass. The quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

The dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo means goods carried together. The wreck was found in the late 1990s. It showed that Vietnam made a huge number of glazed dishes.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Objects can connect places far apart. People make, carry, exchange and use objects. Ceramics are things made of fired clay. They are good evidence. Fired clay lasts long, and people made lots of it. Makers in Southeast Asia had an important part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York has a picture of a bird among clouds. The dish is from the early part of 1500 to 1599. The museum says it was probably made in Hai Duong in Vietnam. This is an attribution, or origin. It is a carefully reasoned idea about where the work was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny glass-like layer. Quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

This dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo is goods carried together. The wreck was found in the late 1990s. It shows Vietnam made huge numbers of glazed dishes.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Vietnamese ceramics made for use at home and for export. Indonesia was a market for Chinese and Southeast Asian wares. Vietnamese makers produced vessels shaped like animals as well as dishes. They also made tiles used on Indonesian mosques and other buildings. Exchange connected objects for the home, decoration on buildings and religious settings. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the pictured dish, or where it was going.

Making ceramics also had a local history. Under the early Lê dynasty, in the fifteenth century, policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities supplied different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bát Tràng, near Hanoi, and Nam Sách in Hải Dương as important centres for blue-and-white ceramics. Makers there supplied everyday vessels and special forms for buyers at home and overseas. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made choices. It was not just a stopping point between other societies. Still, this does not prove which kiln, or pottery oven, made this dish.

The dish's materials explain part of how it looks. Cobalt gives the blue decoration, and the clear glaze lets the brushwork show. People in a workshop worked together on shaping, decorating and firing. Making many vessels did not make each person's skill disappear. A workshop joined learned artistic knowledge to the practical work of supplying goods.
read.sections.1.text.note: Bát Tràng as บัตจ่าง, Nam Sách as นามซัก, Lê dynasty as ราชวงศ์เล; blue-and-white ceramics as เครื่องลายครามสีน้ำเงินขาว (เครื่องลายคราม alone already means blue-and-white ware). kiln as เตาเผา. Check spellings.
read.sections.1.text.back:
This dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records that Vietnamese ceramics of the 15th and 16th centuries were made both for use at home and for export. Indonesia was a market for ceramics from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers produced both dishes and animal-shaped vessels. They also made tiles used in mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. Exchange linked household goods, building decoration and religious places. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the dish in the picture or where it was going.

Pottery making also had a local history. In the early Le dynasty in the 15th century, policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities produced for different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bat Trang, near Hanoi, and Nam Sach in Hai Duong as important centres of blue-and-white porcelain. Makers there produced everyday vessels and special forms for buyers at home and abroad. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made their own decisions, not just a stopping point between other societies. Even so, this does not prove which kiln, or oven for firing pottery, this dish came from.

The dish's materials partly explain why it looks the way it does. Cobalt gives the blue of the design, and the clear glaze lets the brushwork show. People in a workshop worked together on shaping, decorating and firing. Making many vessels did not erase individual skill. Workshops joined learned artistic knowledge with the real work of producing goods.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Vietnam was part of a big trade area. The Met says Vietnamese makers made pots for home and to sell abroad. Indonesia bought pots from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made pots shaped like animals. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we do not know who bought this dish. We do not know where it was going.

In the 1400s, the Lê rulers of Vietnam helped craft and trade grow. Some places were known for blue-and-white pots. A museum in Hanoi names two: Bát Tràng and Nam Sách. They made pots for people at home and far away. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not just a stop between other places. But we do not know which oven baked this dish.

The blue paint came from cobalt. The clear glaze lets the brush lines show. In a workshop, people shaped, painted and baked the pots together. They made many pots. But each maker still needed skill.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'The Met says' simplified to พิพิธภัณฑ์ในนิวยอร์กบอกว่า (same museum).
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Vietnam was part of a large trade area. The museum in New York says Vietnamese makers made vessels to use at home and to sell abroad. Indonesia bought vessels from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made animal-shaped vessels. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we don't know who bought this dish. We don't know where the dish was going.

In 1400 to 1499, Vietnam's Le dynasty rulers helped crafts and trade grow. Some places were famous for blue-and-white porcelain. A museum in Hanoi names two places, Bat Trang and Nam Sach. They made vessels for people at home and people far away. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not just a stopping point between other places. But we don't know which kiln fired this dish.

The blue comes from cobalt. The clear glaze lets the brush lines show. In a workshop, people helped each other shape, paint and fire the vessels. They made many vessels, but each maker still needed skill.

read.sections.2.text.source:
A seventeenth-century bronze covered box made in China shows a different connection. Its lid carries an Arabic religious inscription, writing that calls on God's mercy and compassion. The museum places it in the Kangxi period of the Qing dynasty. Chinese making and Arabic religious expression show why a label naming one place cannot describe every relationship in an object. An inscription can be writing and a designed part of a surface at the same time. It does not tell us who used this box, or prove that it was sent abroad.

Exchange was more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers served different uses and audiences. Objects carried designs and religious expressions as well as materials. Particular works reveal these relationships, while parts of their journeys stay uncertain.
read.sections.2.text.note: The Arabic inscription 'calls on God's mercy and compassion': God as พระผู้เป็นเจ้า (KEY_TERMS, L04); a Muslim reader may expect อัลลอฮ์. 'compassion' as ความปรานี because ความกรุณา is blocked by the checker. Kangxi period as สมัยคังซี, Qing as ราชวงศ์ชิง. A reviewer familiar with Islamic Thai usage should read this.
read.sections.2.text.back:
A 17th-century covered bronze box made in China shows another kind of connection. On the lid is a religious inscription in Arabic, a text asking God for mercy and compassion. The museum dates the box to the Kangxi period of the Qing dynasty. Chinese making and religious expression in Arabic show why a label naming one place cannot explain all the relationships in an object. The inscription can be both text and part of the surface design at the same time. It doesn't tell us who used this box and doesn't prove that the box was sent abroad.

Exchange is more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers create work for different uses and audiences. Objects carry not only materials but also designs and religious expression. Each work reveals these relationships, while some parts of its journey remain uncertain.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
A bronze box from China is from the 1600s. It shows a different link. Its lid has writing in Arabic. This writing is an inscription. It asks for God's mercy and kindness. The museum says it was made under the Qing rulers of China. So a box made in China carries Arabic religious words. One place name cannot tell the whole story of an object. The writing is also part of the design. But it does not tell us who used the box. It does not prove the box went abroad.

Trade was more than goods moving on a map. Objects carried designs and beliefs too. They show us links between people. But parts of their journeys stay unknown.
read.sections.2.simpler.note: 'mercy and kindness' of God as ความเมตตาและความเห็นใจ; check this is respectful.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
A bronze box from China is from 1600 to 1699. It shows another kind of connection. On the lid are Arabic letters. These letters are an inscription. It asks God for mercy and sympathy. The museum says the box was made in China's Qing dynasty. So a box made in China has religious words in Arabic. One place name cannot tell an object's whole story. The letters are also part of the design. But they don't tell us who used the box and don't prove the box went abroad.

Trade is more than goods moving on a map. Objects also carry motifs and beliefs. They show us connections between people, but no one knows some parts of their journeys.

write.example.source: The dish shows a connection because it was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that travelled by sea, and that they were part of a big trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who was going to buy it or where the ship was going. We also do not know which kiln made it.
write.example.back: The dish shows a connection because it was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that travelled by sea, and they were part of a large trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who would buy it or where the ship was going. We also still don't know which kiln made this dish.

educatorNotes.0.source: The box's record doesn't show that it was exported or who used it. Keep its inscription and Chinese origin apart from the dish's evidence from a shipwreck cargo; the two are separate works, not goods from the same cargo. Don't treat every shared colour or motif as proof of direct borrowing, and don't translate the inscription beyond the museum's account (a call on God's mercy and compassion).
educatorNotes.0.back: The box's record doesn't show that it was exported or who used it. Keep the box's inscription and Chinese origin apart from the dish's shipwreck-cargo evidence. The two works are separate, not goods from the same ship. Don't treat every shared colour or motif as evidence of direct borrowing, and don't translate the inscription beyond the museum's description (a plea to God for mercy and compassion).

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a connection such as the dish and its cargo, or the box and its Arabic religious writing; a limit such as the buyer, the whole journey, the exact use, or the maker. Accept either object; simple English is fine.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: a connection, such as the dish and the cargo, or the box and the Arabic religious writing; and a limit, such as the buyer, the whole journey, the exact use or the maker. Accept answers about either object. Simple language is fine.

educatorNotes.2.source: Keep "probably" in the dish's attribution to Hai D'uong Province. The Vietnam National Museum of History article (2015) is used only for how craft was organised under the early Lê dynasty, the centres at Bát Tràng and Nam Sách, and demand at home and overseas; its older shipwreck dating and its identification of a named craftswoman aren't used. It doesn't show which kiln made this dish.
educatorNotes.2.back: Keep the word 'probably' in the dish's attribution to Hai Duong province. The Vietnam National Museum of History article (2015) is used only for the organisation of crafts in the early Le dynasty, the centres at Bat Trang and Nam Sach, and demand at home and abroad. The article's older shipwreck dating and its naming of one woman potter are not used. The article doesn't show which kiln made this dish.

educatorNotes.3.source: Vietnamese ceramics for home and export, Indonesia as a market, and Vietnamese tiles on Indonesian buildings come from The Met's record for a separate vessel, the Ewer in the Form of a Phoenix (1992.72.1). It is context, not a third image or a cargo-mate of the dish.
educatorNotes.3.back: Vietnamese ceramics for home use and export, Indonesia as a market, and Vietnamese tiles on Indonesian buildings come from The Met's record for another vessel, Ewer in the Form of a Phoenix (1992.72.1), used as context, not as a third image, and not from the same ship as the dish.

educatorNotes.4.source: The box's image is an older black-and-white photograph from The Met's record; it shows the box's shape and inscription but not its colour.
educatorNotes.4.back: The box image is an old black-and-white photograph from The Met's record. It shows the box's shape and inscription but not its colour.
